name: Dark Citrine
lede: Dark Citrine is a dark shade of [[citrine|citrine]], one of Robert Ridgway's working names built by the plain grammar of modifier plus base color.

sections.title: A modifier, not a new color
sections.body: Dark Citrine joins the modifier *dark* to the base color [[citrine]], a dull yellow-green named for the citrine quartz [1][4]. Ridgway's 1912 plate IV, hue 21, places it well down his tone scale, measured at lightness 45 and a moderate chroma of 30 in LCH terms [1][4]. The ISCC-NBS system groups the same hue block, 107, under 'moderate yellowish brown,' a Delta-E of 9.1 from Ridgway's own point, a reminder that the two systems sort by different rules even when they land in the same neighborhood [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[khaki-olive]] and [[khaki-olive]], at 4.5 and 4.5 ΔE [1][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this shade, as photographed, in 9.7% of 23,781 paintings, 2,307 paintings; within a single canvas it reads as a distinct area in 1,187 of them [3]. That ranks it more common than 92% of the archive's named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1700s, found in 6.8% of that century's 3,449 paintings, 1.4 times the expected rate [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, by lightness rank, in 31% of its appearances [3]. Peter Snayers is its most devoted painter, using it in 9 of his 16 works here, 7.6 times the baseline rate of the museums those paintings come from [3]. The earliest dated appearance is a painting from 916, 996 years before the name's first documented record in 1912; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor and not a first, and the match is a look-alike hue, not proof of pigment [3]. It shares canvases with [[silver-fern]] and [[seaweed-green]] more often than chance, lifts of 5.8 and 4.5 [3]. In printed English the word 'citrine' peaks in the 1920s, counting every sense of the word, so a name that is also a mineral and a fruit can mislead [3].
